chunks: "An op-amp, short for operational amplifier, is a high-gain differential voltage amplifier.

It has two inputs, inverting and non-inverting, and one output, and the output is the difference between the inputs times a huge number, V out equals A(V plus minus V -) , where A is something like a hundred thousand or a million at DC.

Inside, there's a differential input pair that takes the difference, a high-gain stage, and an output stage that can drive a load, plus a small compensation capacitor that rolls the gain off so it stays stable.
On its own that gain is too big to be useful. A millivolt of input difference would try to put hundreds of volts on the output, so it just slams into a supply rail.
The trick is negative feedback: I feed part of the output back to the inverting input.
Now the op-amp adjusts its output until the two inputs are almost equal, and the gain of the whole circuit is set by the feedback resistors, not by the op-amp's own sloppy gain.
That's how you get a precise gain of 10 out of a part whose raw gain might be anywhere from 100 thousand to a million."
